title: Mechatronics
full_title: Mechatronics: Sensors, Actuators and Embedded Control
tagline: Sensors, signal conditioning and data acquisition, microcontrollers, electric motors and drives, hydraulic and pneumatic actuators, and motion control
summary: Mechatronics combines mechanisms, electronics and software into machines that sense and act. The course covers sensors, signal conditioning and data acquisition, microcontrollers and real-time software, DC, stepper and brushless motors and their drives, hydraulic and pneumatic actuation, and closed-loop motion control, ending with the design of complete mechatronic systems.
overview: Mechatronics is the discipline that integrates mechanical engineering, electronics, control theory, and computer science into the design of intelligent machines. The word was coined in 1969 by Tetsuro Mori of Yaskawa Electric Corporation, but the practice is as old as the centrifugal governor: any machine that senses its own state and acts to correct it is a mechatronic system. Today, mechatronics is the dominant design paradigm in manufacturing, automotive, aerospace, medical, and consumer engineering. A modern CNC machine contains over 100 sensors, 20 actuators, 50 microcontrollers, and 10 million lines of code; a modern car contains over 100 ECUs and 150 sensors; a modern robot contains over 50 sensors and 20 actuators.

This course covers the complete mechatronic design chain: sensors and signal conditioning, microcontrollers and embedded software, electric and fluid-power actuators, motion control, and system integration. Each lesson builds on the previous one, and the course ends with the design of complete mechatronic systems. The quantitative tools are the sensor characteristics (accuracy, resolution, bandwidth), the signal conditioning (amplification, filtering, ADC), the microcontroller architecture (CPU, memory, peripherals), the motor theory (torque-speed curve, back-EMF, torque constant), the fluid power (force-velocity curve, valve flow), the motion control (trajectory planning, PID, impedance), and the system integration (architecture, power supply, EMC, reliability).

The course is designed for third-year mechanical engineering students who have completed courses in control systems, electronics, and mechanics of materials. The course assumes familiarity with Laplace transforms, transfer functions, PID control, operational amplifiers, and basic mechanics. The course is not a course in electronics or computer science; it is a course in the integration of electronics, computer science, and mechanics into machines that sense and act.

The course is organized into eight lessons. The first lesson introduces the mechatronic system architecture and the sensor-actuator selection. The second lesson covers sensors for position, force, and temperature measurement. The third lesson covers signal conditioning and data acquisition. The fourth lesson covers microcontrollers and embedded software. The fifth lesson covers electric motors and drives. The sixth lesson covers hydraulic and pneumatic actuators. The seventh lesson covers motion control. The eighth lesson covers system integration, including power supply design, EMC, and reliability analysis.

The course is taught with a strong emphasis on quantitative analysis. Every lesson contains worked examples with numerical answers, exercises with check values, and widget plots that visualize the relationships between the parameters. The course is designed to be self-contained: the student who completes the course will be able to design a complete mechatronic system from the sensor to the actuator, from the signal conditioning to the control algorithm, and from the power supply to the EMC.
outcomes: Select the appropriate sensor for a given application based on accuracy, resolution, bandwidth, linearity, and environment.
Design a signal conditioning circuit with the required gain, bandwidth, CMRR, and anti-aliasing filter for a given sensor.
Select the appropriate microcontroller for a given control application based on execution time, memory, peripherals, and real-time performance.
Calculate the torque-speed curve, back-EMF, and stall torque of a DC motor, and select the appropriate motor drive for a given application.
Calculate the force, velocity, and power of a hydraulic or pneumatic cylinder, and select the appropriate valve for a given application.
Design a trajectory profile (trapezoidal, S-curve) and a PID controller for a given positioning application.
Analyze the electromagnetic compatibility of a mechatronic system and design the grounding, shielding, and filtering to meet the EMC requirements.
Calculate the system reliability and MTBF for a series or parallel redundant system, and design the redundancy to meet the reliability requirements.
Integrate the sensors, signal conditioning, controller, actuator, power supply, and communication into a complete mechatronic system.

chapters.title: Mechatronic systems
chapters.summary: The elements of a mechatronic system, and the circuit basics needed to build one.

chapters.title: Sensors
chapters.summary: Measuring position, speed, acceleration, force, strain, pressure and temperature, and the specifications of sensors.

chapters.title: Signal conditioning and data acquisition
chapters.summary: Operational-amplifier circuits, bridges and filters, noise, analogue-to-digital conversion, sampling and aliasing.

chapters.title: Microcontrollers and embedded software
chapters.summary: Microcontroller architecture, digital input and output, timers, interrupts, pulse-width modulation and real-time programming.

chapters.title: Electric motors and drives
chapters.summary: DC, stepper and brushless motors, their models and torque–speed curves, and H-bridges and motor drives.

chapters.title: Hydraulic and pneumatic actuators
chapters.summary: Pumps, valves, cylinders and motors in fluid-power circuits, and their dynamics.

chapters.title: Motion control
chapters.summary: Closed-loop position and speed control of motor-driven axes, encoders, feedforward and trajectory following.

chapters.title: Designing mechatronic systems
chapters.summary: Integrating sensors, actuators and controllers, safety interlocks, and case studies from printers to vehicles.

history.title: Watt's centrifugal governor
history.detail: James Watt invents the centrifugal governor, the first feedback control system, which is the foundation of mechatronics.

history.title: Faraday's electromagnetic rotation
history.detail: Michael Faraday demonstrates electromagnetic rotation, the foundation of the electric motor.

history.title: Wheatstone bridge
history.detail: Charles Wheatstone publishes the Wheatstone bridge, the foundation of the strain gauge measurement.

history.title: Ziegler-Nichols tuning
history.detail: Ziegler and Nichols publish the Ziegler-Nichols PID tuning method, the most widely used PID tuning method.

history.title: Mechatronics coined
history.detail: Tetsuro Mori of Yaskawa Electric Corporation coins the word 'mechatronics', combining 'mechanics' and 'electronics'.

history.title: Intel 4004 microprocessor
history.detail: Intel introduces the 4004, the first commercial microprocessor, which is the foundation of the microcontroller.

history.title: First autonomous vehicle
history.detail: Carnegie Mellon University develops Navlab, the first autonomous vehicle, which is the foundation of the autonomous vehicle.

history.title: ARM Cortex-M microcontroller
history.detail: ARM introduces the Cortex-M microcontroller, the most widely used microcontroller in embedded systems.
